messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds.
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.
- Do NOT infer or imply causal relationships between components. Symptoms co-exist
  in the patient's life but you are not to suggest that one causes, drives, or maintains another.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers,
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help.
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears,
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed,
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and their consequences should appear as things that happened
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 54
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: North American
  relationship_status: Married
  occupation: Forester
  trauma_type: Accidentally caused serious injury to another
  pcl5: 52

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Triggers: Somatic (Pain): Physical pain in a part of the body, Victim Memories: Reminders of victims, Proximity: Physical proximity
  Threat: Cannot Relax: I am unable to relax even when I know I am in a safe place, Threat from Strangers: I feel threatened by strangers approaching me even in ordinary situations, Watching Others: I watch other people closely for signs that they might harm me
  Memory: Bodily Reenactment: When memories come to mind of what happened, I feel my body is in the same position as when the frightening event occurred., Rage on Recall: When I remember the event I feel intense rage, Grief on Recall: When I remember the event I feel overwhelming grief
  Negative Appraisals: Intrinsic Fault: There is something about me that made the event happen, Can't Rely on Self: I can't rely on myself, No Longer Capable: I am no longer capable of doing the things that defined me

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

# Marcus Webb: A Forester's Reckoning

Marcus Webb was fifty-four when the accident happened, and he had been a forester for thirty-two years. He knew the mountains of western Oregon the way some men know their own houses—the pitch of the terrain, the grain of old growth, the weight of a felled log. On a clear morning in late September, he was working with his crew on a steep slope above the Cascades, marking timber for harvest. His apprentice, a twenty-three-year-old named Danny Reeves, was newer to the work but steady. Marcus had trained him for two seasons and trusted him enough to work the lower section while Marcus moved upslope to assess a stand of Douglas fir.

What happened in the next forty minutes would remake Marcus's understanding of himself. A massive hemlock, weakened by disease and hidden rot, came down in a direction no one had predicted. Marcus heard the crack and the terrible whistle of its fall, but by the time he turned and saw Danny below him—Danny who had stepped into the tree's path while measuring—there was nothing to do but watch. The hemlock struck Danny across the pelvis and left leg, crushing him against the rocky ground. Marcus reached him within seconds, but the weight of the tree had already done its work. Danny's screams, the blood pooling beneath him, the way his left leg bent at an angle that made Marcus's stomach turn—all of it burned into Marcus's mind with the clarity of a photograph held too close to a flame.

In the hospital that night, Marcus learned that Danny had survived but would likely never walk without significant difficulty. The femur was shattered in three places. There would be surgeries, months of rehabilitation, and permanent nerve damage. Danny's family came from Portland, and when his mother looked at Marcus in the waiting room, he saw in her face the full weight of what he had done.

The months that followed were a slow erosion. Marcus returned to work after six weeks, because stopping felt like surrender, but the forest had become a place of terror. Pain—the phantom sensation of being crushed himself—would seize him without warning. A sharp twinge in his own leg or hip would send him into a state of alarm, certain that his body was remembering what had happened, that he was somehow reliving Danny's injury through his own flesh. He began to notice other foresters on the job site differently, watching them for any sign of carelessness or blame in their eyes. When a stranger approached him at the hardware store in town to ask directions, Marcus's chest tightened and he found himself scanning the man's face for hostility, certain without reason that this person knew what he had done and meant him harm.

At night, he would lie rigid in bed next to his wife, Sarah, unable to relax even in the darkness of their bedroom, even when he consciously reminded himself that no tree was falling, that he was safe. His body refused to believe him. When sleep came, it brought memories so vivid that he would wake with his arms braced as if to block a falling trunk, his muscles locked in the exact posture of that moment on the slope when he realized what was happening and could do nothing.

The anger came without warning and with terrible force. Thinking of that morning—of his own failure to predict the tree's fall, his own miscalculation—would flood him with a rage so intense that he had thrown a coffee mug against the kitchen wall. Sarah had flinched. But worse than the anger was the grief that followed it, a crushing weight that made him weep in his truck during lunch breaks, mourning not only Danny's future but his own. He had come to believe, with a certainty that felt immovable, that something in him was fundamentally wrong—something that made disaster inevitable when he was in charge. He could no longer trust himself to make sound decisions. The work that had defined him, that had given his life meaning and structure for three decades, now felt like proof of his incapacity. He was no longer the careful, capable man he had believed himself to be. He was someone who destroyed things.

It was Sarah who finally insisted he see someone. She had watched him withdraw from his crew, watched him turn down a promotion to supervisor—a position he would have once fought for—watched him sit at the kitchen table for hours without speaking. She was afraid of what his silence meant. Marcus came to his first appointment reluctant, certain that talking could not undo what he had done, but desperate enough to try.
